hook.text: An app asks to access your Google photos. You click Allow without giving it your Google password. That's OAuth.

buildup.text: OAuth lets you grant limited access to your data on one service to another service, without sharing credentials.

discovery.text: The flow issues a token with specific scopes: 'read photos' but not 'delete account.' Fine-grained control.

twist.text: OAuth handles authorization, not authentication. OpenID Connect adds identity on top — proving who you are.

climax.text: Every 'Sign in with Google' or 'Login with GitHub' button uses OAuth or OpenID Connect behind the scenes.

punchline.text: OAuth shares access, not passwords. Trust with limits.

quiz.question: What does OAuth handle?
options: Authorization — granting limited access without sharing passwords

details.summary: OAuth is an authorization framework that lets applications access user resources on other services without sharing passwords.
details.whyItMatters: OAuth enables the modern connected web where applications securely share data. Every time you log in with Google or connect apps to your accounts, OAuth is the mechanism making it safe.
takeaways: OAuth issues tokens instead of sharing user passwords
Scopes limit what an application can access
Access tokens expire and refresh tokens enable renewal

faq.question: What is the difference between OAuth and OpenID Connect?
faq.answer: OAuth handles authorization — granting access to resources. OpenID Connect builds on OAuth to add authentication — verifying who the user is. When you sign in with Google, OpenID Connect proves your identity. When an app requests access to your Google Drive, OAuth grants that access.

faq.question: What are OAuth scopes?
faq.answer: Scopes define the specific permissions an application requests, like read-only email access or full calendar management. Users see the requested scopes in the consent screen and can approve or deny. Well-designed applications request only the minimum scopes needed for their functionality.
